examples.starter.title: Practice
examples.starter.description: Now it's time to do some practice to consolidate what we've learned.
examples.finish.title: Practice completed!
steps.starter.title: Intro
steps.starter.description: Regex is short for `Regular Expression`. It helps to match, find or manage text. The lessons and the Playground use JavaScript's regex engine, where a pattern is written as `/pattern/flags`. Start by typing `OK` in the Regex field to proceed to the first step and access the more detailed description.
steps.whatIsRegex.title: What are Regular Expressions `Regex`?
steps.whatIsRegex.description: Regular Expressions are a string of characters that express a search pattern. They are often abbreviated as `Regex` or `Regexp`. They are especially used to find or replace words in texts. In addition, we can test whether a text complies with the rules we set.\n\n For example, let's say you have a list of filenames. And you only want to find files with the `pdf` extension. Then typing an expression like `^\w+\.pdf$` will do the job. The meaning of the definitions in this expression will become clearer as the steps progress.
steps.basicMatchers.title: Basic Matchers
steps.basicMatchers.description: The character or word we want to find is written directly, just like a normal search. For example, to find the word `curious` in the text, type it as it is.
steps.dotCharacter.title: Dot `.`: Any Character
steps.dotCharacter.description: The period `.` allows selecting any character, including special characters and spaces. Type a period `.` in the Regex field to proceed.
steps.characterSet.title: Character Sets `[abc]`
steps.characterSet.description: If a character in a word can be one of several characters, we write all the alternatives inside square brackets `[]`. For example, to write an expression that finds all the words in the text, type the characters `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u` next to each other inside the square brackets `[]`.
steps.negatedCharacterSet.title: Negated Character Sets `[^abc]`
steps.negatedCharacterSet.description: To find all words in the text below, except for `ber` and `bor`, type `e` and `o` side by side after the caret `^` character inside square brackets `[]`.
steps.range.title: Letter Range `[a-z]`
steps.range.description: To find letters in a range, we write the first and last letters inside square brackets `[]` with a dash `-` between them. It is case-sensitive. Type the expression that selects all lowercase letters from `e` to `o`, including `e` and `o`.
steps.rangeNumber.title: Number Range `[0-9]`
steps.rangeNumber.description: To find digits in a range, we write the first and last digits inside square brackets `[]` with a dash `-` between them. Type the expression that selects all digits from `3` to `6`, including `3` and `6`.
examples.basicMatchers.title: Practice: Basic Matcher
examples.basicMatchers.description: Write the expression that selects every `of` in the text.
examples.dotCharacter.title: Practice: Any Character
examples.dotCharacter.description: Type the expression to select individual letters, numbers, spaces, and special characters in the text. The expression you type must match any character.
examples.characterSet.title: Practice: Character Sets
examples.characterSet.description: Write the expression that matches each word in the text. The only character that changes is the first letter of each word.
examples.negatedCharacterSet.title: Practice: Negated Character Sets
examples.negatedCharacterSet.description: Write the expression that matches every word in the text except `beor` and `beur`. Use a negated character set to do this.
examples.range.title: Practice: Letter Range
examples.range.description: Write the expression that selects the letters from `g` to `k` in the text.\n`g` and `k` should also be included in the range.
examples.rangeNumber.title: Practice: Number Range
examples.rangeNumber.description: Write the expression that selects the digits from `2` to `7` in the text.\n`2` and `7` should also be included in the range.
steps.repetitions.title: Repetitions
steps.repetitions.description: Some special characters are used to specify how many times a character can repeat, or whether it appears at all. These special characters are the plus `+`, the asterisk `*` and the question mark `?`.
steps.asterisk.title: Asterisk `*`
steps.asterisk.description: We put an asterisk `*` after a character to indicate that the character may either not match at all or can match many times. For example, indicate that the letter `e` may not occur in the text at all, or may occur once or more side by side.
steps.plusCharacter.title: Plus Sign `+`
steps.plusCharacter.description: To indicate that a character must occur one or more times, we put a plus sign `+` after a character. For example, indicate that the letter `e` must occur one or more times in the text.
steps.questionMark.title: Question Mark `?`
steps.questionMark.description: To indicate that a character is optional, we put a `?` question mark after a character. For example, indicate that the following letter `u` is optional.
steps.quantifier.title: Curly Braces - 1
steps.quantifier.description: To require a character to occur a specific number of times, we write that number in curly braces `{n}` right after it. For example, indicate that the following letter `e` must occur exactly `2` times in a row.
steps.quantifierMin.title: Curly Braces - 2
steps.quantifierMin.description: To require a character to occur at least a certain number of times, we write that number followed by a comma inside curly braces `{n,}` right after it. For example, indicate that the following letter `e` must occur at least `3` times in a row.
steps.quantifierRange.title: Curly Braces - 3
steps.quantifierRange.description: To require a character to occur within a range of times, we write the minimum and maximum inside curly braces `{x,y}` right after it; both limits are inclusive. For example, indicate that the following letter `e` must occur between `1` and `3` times in a row.
examples.asterisk.title: Practice: Asterisk `*`
examples.asterisk.description: Use the asterisk `*` to write the expression that will select each word where the letter `e` is absent or is present one or more times.
examples.plusCharacter.title: Practice: Plus Sign `+`
examples.plusCharacter.description: Write the expression using the plus sign `+` to select words in which the letter `e` occurs one or more times in the text.
examples.questionMark.title: Practice: Question Mark `?`
examples.questionMark.description: Write the expression indicating that the letter `n` is optional in the text, using the question mark `?`. Thus, both the words `a` and `an` can be selected.
examples.quantifier.title: Practice: Curly Braces - 1
examples.quantifier.description: Write the expression that finds numbers made of `4` digits in a row, using curly braces `{}`. Remember that the range `[0-9]` matches a single digit.
examples.quantifierMin.title: Practice: Curly Braces - 2
examples.quantifierMin.description: Write the expression that finds numbers with at least `2` digits in a row, using curly braces `{}`.
examples.quantifierRange.title: Practice: Curly Braces - 3
examples.quantifierRange.description: Write the expression that finds numbers with at least `1` and at most `4` digits in a row, using curly braces `{}`.
steps.grouping.title: Parentheses `( )`: Grouping
steps.grouping.description: We can group an expression and then reference the group or apply rules to it. To group an expression, we put it in parentheses `()`. For now, just group `haa` below.
steps.groupReference.title: Referencing a Group
steps.groupReference.description: Below, we have two groups: `(ha)` and `(haa)`. When we want to reference these groups later in the pattern, we use `\1` for the first group and `\2` for the second group. For example, in the pattern `(ha)-\1,(haa)-\2`, the `-` is outside the groups, and `\1` refers to `ha` while `\2` refers to `haa`. Type `\2` at the end of the expression to refer to the second group.
steps.nonCapturingGrouping.title: Parentheses `(?: )`: Non-capturing Grouping
steps.nonCapturingGrouping.description: Adding `?:` right after the opening parenthesis, like `(?:ha)`, makes a group non-capturing: it still groups the expression, but its match is not stored, so it cannot be referenced. Below, the first group `(?:ha)` is non-capturing. That is why the reference `\1` refers to the capturing group `(haa)`. Type `\1` at the end of the expression to reference the grouped `haa`.
steps.pipeCharacter.title: Pipe Character `|`
steps.pipeCharacter.description: It lets you specify that an expression can be one of several different expressions. All possible expressions are written separated by the pipe sign `|`. This differs from a character set `[abc]`: character sets operate at the character level. Alternatives are at the expression level. For example, the following expression would select both `cat` and `rat`. Add another pipe sign `|` to the end of the expression and type `dog` so that all words are selected.
steps.escapeCharacter.title: Escape Character `\`
steps.escapeCharacter.description: Some characters have a special meaning in regex: `{ } [ ] ( ) / \ + * . $ ^ | ?` To match these characters themselves, we need to put an escape character `\` before them. For example, to select the dot `.` and asterisk `*` characters in the text, add an escape character `\` before each of them.
steps.caret.title: Caret Sign `^`:\nSelecting by Line Start
steps.caret.description: We were using `[0-9]` to find digits. To find only the digits at the beginning of a line, put the `^` sign at the start of this expression.
steps.dollar.title: Dollar Sign `$`:\nSelecting by End of Line
steps.dollar.description: Add the `$` sign after `html` to find `html` only at the end of a line.
steps.wordCharacter.title: Word Character `\w`: Letter, Number and Underscore
steps.wordCharacter.description: The expression `\w` is used to find letters, numbers and underscore characters. Let's use the expression `\w` to find word characters in the text.
steps.withoutWordCharacter.title: Non-word Characters `\W`
steps.withoutWordCharacter.description: The expression `\W` is used to find characters other than letters, numbers, and underscores.
steps.numberCharacter.title: Digit Character `\d`
steps.numberCharacter.description: `\d` is used to find only digits.
steps.withoutNumberCharacter.title: Non-digit Characters `\D`
steps.withoutNumberCharacter.description: `\D` is used to find any character that is not a digit.
steps.spaceCharacter.title: Whitespace Character `\s`
steps.spaceCharacter.description: `\s` is used to find only whitespace characters, such as spaces, tabs and line breaks.
steps.withoutSpaceCharacter.title: Non-whitespace Characters `\S`
steps.withoutSpaceCharacter.description: `\S` is used to find any character that is not whitespace.
steps.lookarounds.title: Lookarounds
steps.lookarounds.description: If we want an expression to match only when it comes before or after another expression, we use lookarounds. Continue to the next step to learn how they work.
steps.positiveLookahead.title: Positive Lookahead: `(?=)`
steps.positiveLookahead.description: For example, we want to select the hour value in the text. To select only the numbers followed by `PM`, we write the positive lookahead `(?=)` after our expression. Add `PM` after the `=` sign inside the parentheses.
steps.negativeLookahead.title: Negative Lookahead: `(?!)`
steps.negativeLookahead.description: For example, we want to select the numbers in the text other than the hour value. To select only the numbers not followed by `PM`, we write the negative lookahead `(?!)` after our expression. Add `PM` after the `!` sign inside the parentheses.
steps.positiveLookbehind.title: Positive Lookbehind: `(?<=)`
steps.positiveLookbehind.description: For example, we want to select the price value in the text. To select only the numbers preceded by `$`, we write the positive lookbehind `(?<=)` before our expression. Add `\$` after the `=` sign inside the parentheses.
steps.negativeLookbehind.title: Negative Lookbehind: `(?<!)`
steps.negativeLookbehind.description: For example, we want to select the numbers in the text other than the price value. To select only the numbers not preceded by `$`, we write the negative lookbehind `(?<!)` before our expression. Add `\$` after the `!` sign inside the parentheses.
steps.flags.title: Flags
steps.flags.description: Flags change how an expression matches, which is why they are also called `modifiers`. They determine whether the expression treats the text as separate lines, whether it is case-sensitive, and whether it finds all matches. Continue to the next step to learn about flags.
steps.flagsGlobal.title: Global Flag
steps.flagsGlobal.description: The `global` flag makes the expression select all matches. If it is not used, only the first match is selected. Now enable the `global` flag to select all matches.
steps.flagsMultiline.title: Multiline Flag
steps.flagsMultiline.description: By default, regex treats the whole text as a single line. The `multiline` flag makes it handle each line separately, so expressions that use the start `^` or end `$` of a line work for every line. Now enable the `multiline` flag to find all matches.
steps.flagsCaseInsensitive.title: Case-insensitive Flag
steps.flagsCaseInsensitive.description: To make the expression ignore the difference between uppercase and lowercase letters, enable the `case-insensitive` flag.
steps.greedyMatching.title: Greedy Matching
steps.greedyMatching.description: Regex does greedy matching by default, which means a match is as long as possible. Look at the example below: it matches anything that ends with `r` and is preceded by any characters, but it does not stop at the first `r`.
steps.lazyMatching.title: Lazy Matching
steps.lazyMatching.description: Lazy matching, unlike greedy matching, stops at the first possible match. In the example below, add a `?` after `*` to find the first match that ends with the letter `r` and is preceded by any characters. This makes the match stop at the first `r`.
steps.completeAllSteps.title: Congratulations, you have completed all the steps!
steps.completeAllSteps.description: You can return to the previous steps whenever you want, and you can easily navigate through all the steps you have passed.
